The source is computed by the double complex of smooth forms \(\mathcal A^{j,i}_{\widetilde X}(\log E)=\Omega ^{j}_{\widetilde X}(\log E)\otimes \mathcal A^{0,i}_{\widetilde X}\), for \(j\ge p\), with the differentials \(\partial \) and \(\bar\partial \). For the target, let \(\mathcal D^{j,i}_X\) be the sheaf of currents of type \((j,i)\), put \(a=j-p+1\), and let \(\mathcal C^{j,i}=\mathcal D^{j,i}_X\otimes \mathcal O_X(a\cdot T)\) for \(j\ge p\). For a local equation \(g\) of \(T\), a section of \(\mathcal C^{j,i}\) is \(S\otimes g^{-a}\) for a unique current \(S\). The differentials are \(\bar\partial S\otimes g^{-a}\) and

\[
\begin{gathered}
\nabla (S\otimes g^{-a})=(g\cdot \partial S-a\cdot \partial g\wedge S)\otimes g^{-(a+1)}.
\end{gathered}
\]

The second is the formula for the derivative of \(S/g^{a}\). It does not depend on \(g\), it squares to zero, and it anticommutes with \(\bar\partial \). By the second fact, the column \(\mathcal C^{j,\bullet }\) resolves \(\Omega ^{j}_X(a\cdot T)\), and on these subsheaves \(\nabla \) is the exterior derivative. So the total complex of \(\mathcal C\) computes the hypercohomology of \(P^{p}\Omega ^{\bullet}_X(*T)\).

A current \(S\) on \(\widetilde X\) has a pushforward, defined by \(\langle \pi _*S,\varphi \rangle =\langle S,\pi ^{*}\varphi \rangle \) for test forms \(\varphi \) on \(X\). The pushforward preserves the type, commutes with \(\partial \) and \(\bar\partial \), and satisfies the projection formula \(\pi _*(\pi ^{*}u\wedge S)=u\wedge \pi _*S\) for a smooth form \(u\). Since \(\pi \) is birational, \(\pi _*\pi ^{*}\alpha =\alpha \) for every smooth form \(\alpha \) on \(X\).

Let \(\eta \) be a section of \(\mathcal A^{j,i}_{\widetilde X}(\log E)\) over the preimage of an open set on which \(g\) is defined. The function \(\pi ^{*}g\) vanishes on \(E\) and \(\eta \) has at most simple poles along \(E\), so \(\pi ^{*}g^{a}\cdot \eta \) is a smooth form. Put

\[
\begin{gathered}
\pi _\sharp (\eta )=\pi _*(\pi ^{*}g^{a}\cdot \eta )\otimes g^{-a}.
\end{gathered}
\]

This does not depend on \(g\), and it commutes with \(\bar\partial \) because \(\pi ^{*}g\) is holomorphic. In \(\nabla \pi _\sharp (\eta )\) the two terms containing \(\partial g\) cancel, by the product rule and the projection formula, and what remains is

\[
\begin{gathered}
\nabla \pi _\sharp (\eta )=\pi _*(\pi ^{*}g^{a+1}\cdot \partial \eta )\otimes g^{-(a+1)}=\pi _\sharp (\partial \eta ).
\end{gathered}
\]

So \(\pi _\sharp \) is a map of double complexes. Let \(\mu \) be the map it induces. For a smooth form \(\alpha \) on \(X\) of type \((j,i)\),

\[
\begin{gathered}
\pi _\sharp (\pi ^{*}\alpha )=g^{a}\cdot \pi _*\pi ^{*}\alpha \otimes g^{-a}=\alpha \otimes 1.
\end{gathered}
\]

Hence \(\mu \) composed with the pullback is the map induced by the inclusion of \(\sigma _{\ge p}\Omega ^{\bullet}_X\) in \(P^{p}\Omega ^{\bullet}_X(*T)\). The image of \(c\) is therefore \(\mu (\widetilde c)=0\). ∎

In the language of mixed Hodge modules, the lemma combines the strictness of the Hodge filtration under projective direct image with the bound \(\mathcal F_{k}\mathcal O_X(*T)\subset \mathcal O_X((k+1)T)\) of [Mustaţă–Popa, Hodge ideals, equation (0.1)](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~mpopa/papers/SI.pdf).

*Conclusion.* Each \(K^{j}\) has zero higher cohomology. Indeed, in

\[
\begin{gathered}
0 \to  \Omega ^{j}_P(a_jR) \to  \Omega ^{j}_P(a_j(X+R)) \to  K^{j} \to  0
\end{gathered}
\]

both twists are positive because \(a_j\ge 1\) and \(e>0\). Bott vanishing and the long exact sequence give the claim. Hence \(\mathbb H^{n}(P,K^{\bullet} )\) is computed by global sections. The zero class of the top section \(\omega _A\) supplies a global section \(\overline{\beta }\) of \(K^{n-1}\) with \(d\overline{\beta }=\omega _A\). The same sequence in degree \(n-1\), and \(H^{1}(P,\Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot R))=0\), lift it to

\[
\begin{gathered}
\beta  \in  H^{0}(P,\Omega ^{n-1}_P(q\cdot X+q\cdot R)).
\end{gathered}
\]

Thus \(\omega _A-d\beta \) has poles only on \(R\). In particular, the primitive has at most \(q\)-fold poles along every component of \(R\) and along \(X\), with no added support.

The paragraph on forms and fields, with \(m=q\), turns \(\beta \) into a certificate with denominator \(D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\). This proves \(1\Longrightarrow 3\). The implication \(3\Longrightarrow 2\) is immediate, and \(2\Longrightarrow 1\) is the residue argument already given. Multiplying \(N\) by \((D/D_{\mathrm{red}})^q\) gives the prescribed denominator \(D^q\). Averaging the field under \(\tau \) preserves this even denominator and the target, and enforces the component parities. It can also retain \(D_{\mathrm{red}}^q\), since stability of its reduced support implies \(D_{\mathrm{red}}\circ \tau =\pm D_{\mathrm{red}}\). Finally, the fixed-denominator normalized equations form a finite linear system over the original coefficient field. Consistency over \(\mathbb C\) implies consistency over that field by Gaussian elimination. ∎

This also proves the claimed necessity of certificates for an arbitrary divisor support: choose an ambient \(D\) cutting that divisor, apply the theorem, and use the resulting polynomial tuple. If the original coefficients lie in a smaller field, the descent argument below gives a certificate over that field, possibly with a different support. The proof bounds poles on a chosen support; it supplies no bound on the degree \(e\) of the support itself.

At **\(q=1\)**, therefore, existence over \(D\) is equivalent to existence over any \(D^{m}\). An exact failure of the full fixed-\(D\) linear system excludes every higher power of that \(D\). At **\(q=2\)**, the definitive test on its support uses \(D^{2}\). Failure over \(D\) alone need not exclude support.

The distinction is sharp. Set

\[
\begin{gathered}
D=X_{0}^{6}+X_{1}^{6}+X_{2}^{6},       E=Y_{0}^{6}+Y_{1}^{6}+Y_{2}^{6},       F=D+E,\\
A=X_{0}^{3}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{3}\cdot Y_{0}\cdot Y_{1}\cdot Y_{2},       q=2.
\end{gathered}
\]

Writing \(\epsilon _X\) and \(\epsilon _Y\) for the two block Euler fields, the strict certificate is

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=A(F\epsilon _X-D\cdot \epsilon _Y)/(12\cdot D^{2}).
\end{gathered}
\]

For the numerator \(N_{2}=A(F\epsilon _X-D\cdot \epsilon _Y)/12\), direct blockwise differentiation gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
2\cdot N_{2}(F)=A\cdot D^{2},       \operatorname{div} N_{2}=A\cdot F,       N_{2}(D^{2})=A\cdot F\cdot D^{2}.
\end{gathered}
\]

These identities prove both normalized equations, with \(E_{2}\) identically zero. The field has degree seven and the required parities. Fermat smoothness is immediate from its partial derivatives, and \(D\) is coprime to \(F\) because \(D\) and \(E\) involve disjoint variables and have no common factor.

There is no numerator over \(D\). To prove this without an ansatz, normalize \(E_{1}\) and average a hypothetical numerator over the six independent sixth-root coordinate scalings, projecting onto the character of \(A\). Both \(F\) and \(D\) are invariant, so this operation preserves the fixed denominator and the two equations. The retained monomials in \(N_{i}\) have exponent vector congruent modulo six to \((3,3,3,1,1,1)+e_{i}\). These six residues are all less than six and already sum to the required numerator degree thirteen. Thus \(N_{i}=c_{i}AZ_{i}\) is the entire surviving space, not a selected family. \(E_{1}\) forces \(c_{0}=c_{1}=c_{2}=1/12\) and \(c_{3}=c_{4}=c_{5}=0\). For this numerator, \(\operatorname{div} N=A\) and \(N(D)=A\cdot D/2\), so \(E_{2}\) is \(A\cdot D/2\). It is not divisible even by \(F\). This excludes every original numerator because normalization and averaging preserve existence.

These bounds leave the central search problem untouched: they do not bound the degree of the reduced support that must be found.

## Combining certificates and descending coefficients

For fixed \(F\) and \(q\), the equation is linear in the pair \((A,v)\). If \(v_j\) serves \(A_j\), then \(\sum _{j}c_j\cdot v_j\) serves \(\sum _{j}c_jA_j\). A product of the denominators supplies a common denominator, so supported target spaces add when supports are united. A decomposition into symmetry characters can therefore organize a search without requiring one denominator to serve every component separately.

In cleared form, certificates \((D,N,Q)\) for \(A\) and \((E,M,R)\) for \(B\) combine as

\[
D_{A+B}=DE,\qquad N_{A+B}=EN+DM,\qquad
Q_{A+B}=E^2Q+D^2R.
\]

The resulting defect is \(E^2\mathcal E_A+D^2\mathcal E_B=F^{q+1}(E^2Q+D^2R)\). Nonzero quotient terms therefore cause no obstruction to addition. Denominator legality is preserved by products, and for positive \(q\) each numerator has degree \(\deg D+\deg E+6q-5\).

If \(F\) and \(A\) are rational and \(v\) is defined over a number field \(K\), normalized trace gives a rational certificate:

\[
\begin{gathered}
v_\mathbb Q = \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(v)/[K:\mathbb Q].
\end{gathered}
\]

To prove descent, sum the conjugate fields over all embeddings of \(K\) into a normal closure. Differentiation commutes with each embedding, so each conjugate serves the same \(A\). Their average is Galois-invariant and hence rational. The product of the conjugate denominators is the norm, clears that average, and has degree \([K:\mathbb Q]\operatorname{deg} D\) before cancellation. Each factor is coprime to \(F\), so the norm remains legal. Homogeneity and parity are unchanged.

The same argument works for every finite extension \(K/k\) in characteristic zero. It also suffices to descend an initially complex certificate for data over \(k\). Fix its denominator degree and write the normalized equations in the finitely many coefficients of \(D,N\) and the \(E_{2}\) quotient. These are polynomial equations over \(k\). Legality is an open condition: at least one coefficient of the remainder of \(D\) modulo \(F\) is nonzero. Choose such a coefficient and invert it using one additional variable. A complex point of this finite polynomial system implies a point over an algebraic closure of \(k\), by the Nullstellensatz; its finitely many coordinates generate a finite extension. Trace then gives a certificate over \(k\). This proves descent of existence, without claiming to preserve an initially transcendental supporting equation.

For a bundled target \(A+cB\), with \(1,c\) linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the nondegenerate trace pairing supplies \(p\in K\) satisfying \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p\cdot c)=0\). Indeed, evaluation of that pairing on the independent vectors \(1,c\) defines a surjective linear map \(K\to \mathbb Q^{2}\). Applying trace to the certificate identity for \(p\cdot v\) shows that \(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(p\cdot v)\) serves \(A\). More generally a trace-dual basis extracts every rational component of an extension-field target. Trace over passive function fields appears in Chapter 2, where commutation with the relevant derivatives is proved for that setting.

For completeness, character averaging also has an explicit formula. Suppose a finite diagonal group acts by \(\gamma :Z_{i}\mapsto \gamma _{i}Z_{i}\), with \(F\circ \gamma =\mu _\gamma F\) and \(A\circ \gamma =\nu _\gamma A\). Define

\[
\begin{gathered}
(T_\gamma v)_{i}=\mu _\gamma (v_{i}\circ \gamma )/(\nu _\gamma \gamma _{i}).
\end{gathered}
\]

The chain rule gives \(K_A(T_\gamma v)=K_A(v)\circ \gamma /\nu _\gamma \). Thus averaging \(T_\gamma v\) preserves the certificate and projects onto the required character. A common denominator is the product of the conjugates, so its degree may grow by the group order. This does not justify imposing a single character on \(D\) at a previously chosen degree.

There is a useful exponent description when \(F\) contains all six pure sixth powers. Let \(L(F)\) be the lattice generated by differences of exponents in the support of \(F\). Diagonal substitutions preserving \(F\) up to scalar are exactly the characters of \(\mathbb Z^{6}/L(F)\). Modulo global scalar substitutions this is a finite group: the six pure powers force all \(\gamma _{i}^{6}\) to agree, and a common scalar makes them all one. Characters separate its exponent cosets at fixed degree. For a character field component, reduced numerator and denominator are both eigenvectors: the identity obtained by transforming their coprime quotient forces each factor to be carried to a scalar multiple of itself. Their characters differ by that of \(A\) times the \(i\)-th coordinate divided by the character of \(F\). This proves the support-coset rule without discarding rational fields, though averaging may increase degree.

For a full-support \(Y\)-even sextic, \(L(F)\) is exactly the lattice of vectors of total sum zero and even \(Y\)-sum. One inclusion follows from parity. Conversely, exponent differences realize all within-\(X\) and within-\(Y\) coordinate transfers, and also \(2(e_{X_{i}}-e_{Y_{j}})\); these generate that lattice. Hence all \(Y\)-odd targets of one degree belong to a single coset. Fine target-character decompositions are a property of structured \(F\), not an available simplification for general \(F\).

## Jacobian reduction and exact verification

Let \(J(F)=(\partial _{0}F,\ldots ,\partial _{5}F)\). If \(A=\sum _{i}G_{i}\partial _{i}F\), taking \(v=G/q\) gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
K_A(G/q)=F\cdot \operatorname{div}(G)/q.
\end{gathered}
\]

This lowers the pole order by one: modulo an exact form, \(\omega _A\) becomes \((\operatorname{div} G/q)\Omega /F^q\). Membership in \(J(F)\) therefore kills the leading Hodge-graded piece; it need not kill the whole residue class. For invariant \(q=1\) targets it does kill the class: the lower contribution would lie in the anti-invariant (4,0) space. Equivalently, after parity averaging, \(\operatorname{div}(G)\) is a \(Y\)-odd constant and hence zero.

For a concrete \(q=2\) example in our diagonal involution coordinates, take Fermat \(F\) and

\[
\begin{gathered}
A=6\cdot X_{0}^{6}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0},       G_{0}=X_{0}\cdot X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0},       G_{i}=0 \;\text{for}\; i>0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Then \(A=\sum G_{i}\partial _{i}F\) is \(Y\)-odd and belongs to \(J(F)\), but one reduction gives the \(q=1\) numerator \(X_{1}^{3}\cdot X_{2}^{2}\cdot Y_{0}/2\). All of its exponents are at most four, so it is nonzero in the Fermat Jacobian ring \(\mathbb C[Z]/(Z_{0}^{5},\ldots ,Z_{5}^{5})\). Griffiths's graded isomorphism makes its (3,1) class nonzero. Thus the original \(q=2\) residue is nonzero, despite Jacobian membership. A complete reduction algorithm must retain this lower-pole target.

For an explicit field, clearing denominators reduces verification to polynomial identities and the homogeneity and coprimality conditions. A nonzero remainder divisible by \(F^{q+1}\) is valid. [Chapter 5](#technical-information/computation) gives the complete polynomial criterion and proves equivalence with strict existence when the denominator may change.

# 3. Geometric support, finite groups and surface fibrations

[Previous: binary sextics and torsion contacts](#technical-information/binary-blocks) · [Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: split sextics and K3 correspondences](#technical-information/split-and-k3)

A certificate constructs a primitive on the complement of a divisor. Geometry establishes the same vanishing through Gysin maps and correspondences. This chapter develops the shared tools: finite quotients, correspondences over a common base, two-forms on curve families, covering rational curves, surface fibrations with \(p_g=q=0\), and supported projectors in families. The reflection and relative-projector results supply the two parts of [Chapter 3B](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds). Fano support and correspondence transfer also underlie the quadratic-net theorem of [Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets). Work in characteristic zero; cohomology is rational, or algebraic de Rham after scalar extension.

## 3.1 Divisor support and its source

For a smooth projective variety \(X\), a class is divisor-supported if it vanishes on \(X\setminus Z\) for some divisor \(Z\). The resulting subspace is \(N^{1}H^{k}(X)\). Here is the Gysin description of that space. Take an embedded resolution \(r:\widetilde{X}\to X\) whose reduced inverse image \(E=\bigcup E_i\) is a simple normal-crossing divisor. Localization places \(r^{*}\alpha \) in the image of \(H^{k}_E(\widetilde{X})\to H^{k}(\widetilde{X})\). The Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence for supports and purity give, for an intersection of \(c\) components, the terms \(H^{k-c-1}(E_{i_{1}}\cap \cdots \cap E_{i_c})(-c)\) contributing to degree \(k\). Their weights are \(k+c-1\). The \(c=1\) terms have weight \(k\), while all deeper intersections have larger weight. Strictness of mixed-Hodge morphisms therefore makes the image in the pure \(H^{k}(\widetilde{X})\) equal to the image of \(\sum _i H^{k-2}(E_i)(-1)\). Push forward and use \(r_*r^{*}=\operatorname{id}\). This proves that \(N^{1}H^{k}(X)\) is generated by the resulting proper Gysin images from smooth divisors. The localization, purity and strictness inputs are stated in [Chapter 1](#technical-information/certificates).

On a fourfold the (3,1) part must consequently come from \(H^{2,0}(E_i)\). Components contracted into codimension at least two have zero (3,1) image: degree-four classes supported in codimension two come from degree-zero classes of surfaces with twist \((-2)\), and hence have type (2,2). Thus resolutions of the actual divisor components supply the relevant holomorphic two-forms. A count of singularities or contact multiplicities does not determine their Gysin map.

On a smooth sextic fourfold this forces singularities on any divisor supporting a nonzero (3,1) class. Lefschetz gives \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\mathbb Z[\mathcal O_X(1)]\), so every nonzero effective divisor \(D\) is ample. The sequence \(0\to\mathcal O_X(-D)\to\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_D\to0\), the vanishing \(H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0\), and Kodaira vanishing with Serre duality give \(H^2(D,\mathcal O_D)=0\). If \(D\) is normal with rational singularities, a resolution \(\widetilde D\to D\) has the same coherent cohomology, hence \(H^{2,0}(\widetilde D)=0\). Such a component has zero (3,1) Gysin image. Therefore a support for a nonzero (3,1) class must contain a component which is nonnormal or has nonrational singularities. In particular, replacing a support by a smooth divisor need not preserve its cohomological role.

Support is stable under finite sums: take the union of the supports. For a dominant generically finite proper morphism between smooth varieties of the same dimension, pullback and pushforward preserve divisor support. Pullback uses the inverse image of a support; pushforward uses its proper image, which still has codimension at least one. The degree identity \(p_*p^{*}=\operatorname{deg}(p) \operatorname{id}\) follows from the projection formula.

If a finite group \(G\) acts on a variety \(M\), rational cohomology of the quotient is the invariant cohomology. One proof uses the finite quotient map \(\pi \): the invariant part of \(\pi _*\mathbb Q\) is the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q\), higher direct images vanish, and taking \(G\)-invariants is exact over \(\mathbb Q\). When \(M\) and the quotient are smooth, the corresponding identities are

\[
\begin{gathered}
\pi _*\pi^{*} = |G| \operatorname{id},             \pi^{*}\pi _* = \sum _{g\in G} g^{*}.
\end{gathered}
\]

They also hold for branched quotients: the top-dimensional cycle of \(M\times _{M/G}M\) is the sum of the graphs of the group elements. Their intersections over the branch locus do not add a top-dimensional component.

**Quotient-transfer lemma.** Let \(M\) be smooth projective with a faithful finite \(G\)-action, and let \(N\) be a smooth projective model of \(M/G\). Then \(H^{k}(N)\) is divisor-supported if and only if \(H^{k}(M)^G\) is divisor-supported.

**Proof.** Resolve the quotient rational map equivariantly as \(r:R\to M\) and \(p:R\to N\). Here \(r\) is a sequence of blowups with smooth centers and \(p\) is generically finite of degree \(|G|\). The blowup decomposition

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{k}(\operatorname{Bl}_C M) = H^{k}(M) \oplus  \bigoplus _{j=1}^{\operatorname{codim} C-1} H^{k-2\cdot j}(C)(-j)
\end{gathered}
\]

shows that \(\operatorname{ker} r_*\) is supported on the exceptional divisors. For this formula, write the exceptional divisor as \(E=\mathbb P(N_{C/M})\) and \(\xi =c_{1}(\mathcal O_E(1))\). The added summands map by \(\gamma \mapsto i_*(\xi ^{j-1}\pi^{*}\gamma )\). The projective-bundle decomposition of \(H^{*}(E)\), together with the localization comparison across \(\operatorname{Bl}_C M\setminus E\cong M\setminus C\), gives the displayed decomposition; \(r_*r^{*}=\operatorname{id}\) splits off \(H^{k}(M)\). If \(H^{k}(M)^G\) is supported, then \(r_*p^{*}\beta \) is supported for every \(\beta \in H^{k}(N)\). Hence \(r^{*}r_*p^{*}\beta \) is supported, and \(p^{*}\beta \) differs from it by an exceptional class. Push forward and divide by \(|G|\) to support \(\beta \).

Conversely, take \(\alpha \in H^{k}(M)^G\) and assume \(H^{k}(N)\) is supported. The class \(p^{*}p_*r^{*}\alpha \) is supported. Over the dense open where \(p\) is the finite group quotient, transfer identifies it with \(\sum _g g^{*}r^{*}\alpha =|G|r^{*}\alpha \). Their difference is supported on the omitted boundary, which can be included in a divisor. Push forward by \(r\) and divide by \(|G|\). This proves the lemma and explains why the boundary cannot be dropped. The same proof shows invariance of the all-supported assertion under smooth projective birational modification. ∎

These constructions use algebraic graphs, blowups and traces. An abstract Hodge isomorphism alone would not transport a supporting equation.

### Correspondences over a common base

Let \(M,N\) be smooth projective varieties of the same dimension \(d\). A \(d\)-cycle \(C\subset M\times N\) whose components dominate both factors preserves divisor support:
\[
C_*\bigl(N^1H^k(M)\bigr)\subseteq N^1H^k(N).
\]
Resolve each component of \(C\). Both projections are proper and generically finite. The inverse image of a supporting divisor has dimension at most \(d-1\), and its proper image has dimension at most \(d-1\) as well. Pullback and pushforward through this resolution give the asserted correspondence action. The same argument applies componentwise when \(N\) is disconnected.

**Common-base boundary lemma.** Suppose smooth projective \(d\)-folds \(M_i\) have dominant morphisms to one projective variety \(B\), and all correspondences under consideration lie in the relative products \(M_i\times_B M_j\). Let \(B^\circ\subset B\) be dense open and \(M_i^\circ=M_i\times_B B^\circ\). An identity between the restricted correspondences, or their composites, gives the same identity on global cohomology modulo classes supported on the complement of the output open.

Indeed, if the output point lies over \(B^\circ\), the relative-product condition forces every intermediate point and the input point to lie over \(B^\circ\). Restriction therefore commutes with each proper correspondence action and with its composites. The error operator has image in
\[
\ker\bigl(H^k(M_j)\longrightarrow H^k(M_j^\circ)\bigr).
\]
The complement is a proper closed subset and can be included in a divisor. This proves the claim. The common base is essential to this argument: equality on an arbitrary product open alone does not control contributions from the omitted source.

### Averaging projectors and the part served by a quotient

Let a finite group \(G\) act on a smooth projective variety \(M\), and write
\[
e_K=\frac1{|K|}\sum_{k\in K}k\in\mathbb Q[G]
\]
for a subgroup \(K\). Use \(g\mapsto(g^{-1})^*\) for the left action on cohomology; averaging has the same image under either pullback convention. Suppose smooth projective models of \(M/K_1,\ldots,M/K_s\) have divisor-supported \(H^m\). Form the two-sided ideal
\[
I=\sum_j\mathbb Q[G]e_{K_j}\mathbb Q[G].
\]
Then
\[
I H^m(M)\subseteq N^1H^m(M).
\]
Indeed, quotient transfer supports \(e_{K_j}H^m(M)=H^m(M)^{K_j}\), and \(N^1\) is stable under every group element and under finite sums. This proves the assertion for each product \(a e_{K_j}b\) and hence for \(I\).

Maschke's theorem makes the scope exact at the representation-theoretic level. A simple rational representation \(\rho\) occurs in the ideal \(I\) precisely when \(\rho^{K_j}\ne0\) for at least one \(j\): in its simple algebra factor, \(e_{K_j}\) is nonzero exactly under that condition, and any nonzero element generates the factor as a two-sided ideal. Thus the supported invariant spaces, together with their \(G\)-translates, serve the entire isotypic component of every such \(\rho\). Any projector lying in \(I\) has supported image. This is a criterion for these quotients, not an assertion that the remaining representations lack support from other correspondences.

The same argument applies on a finite auxiliary cover. Resolve a projective model equivariantly, compute the ideal there, and use the proper generically finite map to the original variety. A physical class is served when its pullback lies in the supported image; normalized pushforward then descends the support. Reflections, deck traces and exchanges are instances of this one procedure. Finding more curves on a fixed quotient improves its construction, but cannot add a representation absent from its averaging projector.

### Descent through a deck action and an exchange

Quotients of an auxiliary cover can support complementary parts of the original variety's cohomology. The following criterion isolates the relations needed for their combined descent.

**Proposition.** Let \(p:Z\to X\) be a proper dominant generically finite morphism of smooth complex projective varieties. Let \(d,g\) be finite-order automorphisms of \(Z,X\), respectively; let \(r,\sigma\) be commuting involutions of \(Z\), and \(\tau\) an involution of \(X\). Put \(e=\sigma d\sigma\), and suppose
\[
pd=p,\qquad pe=gp,\qquad pr=\tau p.
\]
If smooth projective models of \(Z/\langle r,\sigma\rangle\) and \(X/\langle g\rangle\) have divisor-supported \(H^k\), then
\[
H^k(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau\subseteq N^1H^k(X,\mathbb Q).
\]

**Proof.** Quotient transfer in §3.1 supports the corresponding invariant spaces. Take \(\xi\in H^k(X)^\tau\), and write \(a=p^*\xi\) in
\[
V=H^k(Z)/N^1H^k(Z).
\]
Then \(d^*a=r^*a=a\). Since \(r,\sigma\) commute, \(p^*\xi+\sigma^*p^*\xi\) is invariant under both; its image \(a+\sigma^*a\) is therefore zero in \(V\). Thus \(\sigma^*a=-a\), which gives
\[
e^*a=\sigma^*d^*\sigma^*a=a.
\]
Let \(\operatorname{Av}_h\) denote averaging over a finite cyclic action. The relation \(pe=gp\) and dominance of \(p\) imply that the order of \(g\) divides that of \(e\), so
\[
a=\operatorname{Av}_e a=p^*(\operatorname{Av}_g\xi)=0
\quad\text{in }V.
\]
The last equality follows from support of \(H^k(X)^{\langle g\rangle}\). Finally, proper pushforward preserves divisor support and \(p_*p^*\xi=\deg(p)\xi\). This proves the claim. ∎

For a rational presentation, apply the criterion after exhibiting a finite symmetry group and resolving its action together with the cover projection equivariantly. Finiteness is a hypothesis to check; individual birational symmetries do not by themselves supply the required models.

## 3.2 Curve correspondences and fibrations

Families of curves on a fourfold give divisor support through their cylinder correspondences. Their action on \(H^{3,1}\) can be tested by a normal-bundle pairing. A covering family of rational curves gives a different conclusion by vanishing on an affine open. Surface fibers with \(p_g=q=0\) give that vanishing after removing finitely many relative divisor classes. These constructions share the support and transfer arguments of §3.1.

### Two-forms on curve families

Let \(X\) be a smooth complex projective fourfold, and let \(\mathcal C\subset S\times X\) be a flat algebraic family whose fibers are smooth connected curves over a dense open of the smooth parameter variety \(S\). The universal cycle associates to \(\omega\in H^{3,1}(X)\) a closed two-form \(\beta_\omega\) on that open. On a smooth projective parameter space its class is the cylinder pullback \(p_*e^*\omega\in H^{2,0}(S)\), where \(p,e\) are the projections of the universal curve.

When \(K_X\simeq\mathcal O_X\), this form has a useful obstruction-theoretic expression. Fix a nonvanishing volume form \(\Omega_X\), embed \(X\) as a smooth divisor in a smooth fivefold \(P\), and let \(C\) be one of the curves. Put \(N=N_{C/X}\), and write

\[
0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow N_{C/P}
\longrightarrow N_{X/P}|_C\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
\delta_C:H^0(C,N_{X/P}|_C)\longrightarrow H^1(C,N).
\]

A section \(A\in H^0(X,N_{X/P})\) gives an embedded Kodaira–Spencer class \(\kappa_A\in H^1(X,T_X)\). Set \(\omega_A=\kappa_A\mathbin{\lrcorner}\Omega_X\). Adjunction identifies \(\det N\) with \(K_C\). For tangent vectors to \(S\) whose normal sections are \(s,t\in H^0(C,N)\),

\[
\boxed{\quad
\beta_{\omega_A}(s,t)
=\operatorname{Tr}_C\bigl(s\wedge t\wedge\delta_C(A|_C)\bigr).
\quad}
\]

The equality uses a fixed choice of signs and normalization of the cycle class. Its nonvanishing is independent of that choice. Equivalently, the right side pairs \(\delta_C(A|_C)\) with \(s\wedge t\in H^0(C,N^\vee\otimes K_C)\) by Serre duality.

**Proof of the formula.** The Hilbert-scheme formula of [Kuznetsov–Markushevich, Theorem 6.1 and formula (25)](https://homepage.mi-ras.ru/~akuznet/publications/SymplecticStructuresOnModuliSpacesOfSheavesViaTheAtyiahClass.pdf) pairs \(s,t,\omega_A|_C\) with the conormal inclusion \(N^\vee\to\Omega_X^1|_C\). For a curve in a fourfold there is one copy of that inclusion. Contracting \(\kappa_A|_C\) with \(\Omega_X\), then applying the conormal inclusion, gives the projection of \(\kappa_A|_C\) to \(H^1(C,N)\), with values in \(\det N\). Naturality of the tangent and normal exact sequences identifies this projection with \(\delta_C(A|_C)\). Wedge with \(s,t\), use \(\det N\simeq K_C\), and take the Serre trace. This is also the infinitesimal expression for the universal-cycle pullback, so it holds after pullback to any smooth algebraic family of curves. ∎

**Curve-family support criterion.** If \(\beta_\omega\) is nonzero on an actual algebraic family, there are a smooth projective surface \(T\) and a cycle \(\Gamma\in\operatorname{CH}^3(T\times X)_{\mathbb Q}\) such that \(\Gamma^*\omega\ne0\) in \(H^{2,0}(T)\). The image of

\[
\Gamma_*:H^2(T,\mathbb Q)(-1)\longrightarrow H^4(X,\mathbb Q)
\]

is divisor-supported and has nonzero \((3,1)\) part.

**Proof.** Close the image of \(S\) in the projective Hilbert scheme of \(X\), take a reduced irreducible component on which the form is nonzero, and resolve it to \(\widetilde M\). Pulling back the universal flat curve gives a cycle in \(\operatorname{CH}^3(\widetilde M\times X)\). Its action gives a global class in \(H^{2,0}(\widetilde M)\) restricting to the displayed two-form. Thus extension across the parameter boundary is supplied by the universal cycle. A general smooth complete-intersection surface \(T\subset\widetilde M\) retains the nonzero class, by weak Lefschetz. Restrict the universal cycle to obtain \(\Gamma\).

Every component of \(\Gamma\) has dimension three, so its proper image in \(X\) is contained in a divisor. Its action therefore vanishes on the complement of that divisor. If \(\eta=\Gamma^*\omega\ne0\), the nonzero pairing \(\int_T\eta\wedge\overline\eta\) equals \(\int_X\omega\wedge\Gamma_*\overline\eta\). Hence \(\Gamma_*\overline\eta\) is a nonzero \((1,3)\) class; conjugation gives the asserted \((3,1)\) image. ∎

This criterion detects a nonzero supported image; at a fixed fourfold it does not assert that the particular input \(\omega\) belongs to that image. For invariant \(\omega\), replace \(\Gamma\) by its average under the involution on \(X\). The pullback of \(\omega\) remains nonzero, and the new image is invariant. [Chapter 4, §4.4](#technical-information/known-locus) gives the further conclusion available when the curve construction dominates the even-sextic coefficient space.

### Vanishing tests for the normal pairing

The normal sections must come from actual motions in a family. A two-dimensional Zariski tangent space at an obstructed point alone does not supply them. On a curve of genus \(g\) in a fourfold with trivial canonical bundle, adjunction and Riemann–Roch give

\[
\chi(N)=1-g.
\]

Thus two independent sections require \(h^1(N)\ge g+1\). A nonzero obstruction space is compatible with a smooth parameter family; requiring \(H^1(N)=0\) would instead make every displayed pairing zero.

**Example: complete-intersection curves.** Suppose \(C=V_X(G_1,G_2,G_3)\) is a smooth complete intersection in a smooth sextic \(X\subset\mathbb P^5\), with \(G_i\) homogeneous of degrees \(d_i\). The regular sequence \((F,G_1,G_2,G_3)\) identifies

\[
N_{C/\mathbb P^5}
\simeq\mathcal O_C(6)\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^3\mathcal O_C(d_i),
\]

and the normal map to \(\mathcal O_C(6)\) is projection to the first summand. Its connecting map \(\delta_C\) is zero. Hence \(\beta_{\omega_A}\) vanishes on every pair of Hilbert tangent directions at \(C\), for every sextic numerator \(A\). This conclusion concerns the whole normal pairing, including motions outside the evident complete-intersection presentation.

**Ambient sections and residual curves.** Let \(T\) be smooth projective, let \(Z\in\operatorname{CH}^2(T\times X)_{\mathbb Q}\) be the class of a family of surfaces, and let \(h\) be a polarization on \(X\). A curve correspondence of the form

\[
\Gamma=(d\,\operatorname{pr}_X^*h+\operatorname{pr}_T^*\ell)\cdot Z,
\qquad \ell\in\operatorname{CH}^1(T),
\]

kills \(H^{3,1}(X)_{\mathrm{prim}}\). Indeed, the projection formula gives

\[
\Gamma^*\alpha=d\,Z^*(h\alpha)+\ell\cup Z^*\alpha=0:
\]

primitivity makes \(h\alpha=0\), while \(Z^*\alpha\) has type \((1,-1)\). This includes relative hypersurface sections of a moving surface family, with a parameter line bundle accounting for the class \(\ell\). If such a section splits into curve correspondences \(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2\), then \(\Gamma_1^*\alpha=-\Gamma_2^*\alpha\). Residual constructions therefore preserve the primitive action up to sign; they cannot create a nonzero action from a component whose action is zero.

More generally, a smooth projective parameter resolution with \(H^{2,0}=0\) cannot carry a nonzero cylinder two-form. This rules out a complete family parametrized by a rational variety even when it contains many moving curves.

### Covering rational curves

**Support theorem.** Let \(W\) be a smooth projective \(n\)-fold, \(n>0\). Suppose an actual morphism \(e:\mathbb P^{1}\times S\to W\) is dominant and generically finite, where \(S\) is smooth integral affine of dimension \(n-1\). Then all \(H^{n}(W)\) is supported on one divisor.

**Proof.** Put \(V=\mathbb A^{1}\times S\). Homotopy invariance and affine de Rham computation give

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{n}_{\mathrm{dR}}(V)=H^{n}_{\mathrm{dR}}(S)=0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Indeed, on \(S\) the de Rham complex is a complex of global sections ending in degree \(n-1\). Compactify \(\mathbb P^{1}\times S\) projectively and take the closure \(\Gamma \) of the graph of \(e\). Its projection \(p:\Gamma \to W\) is proper and generically finite, and \(\Gamma \) contains \(V\) as an open subset. The boundary \(\Gamma \setminus V\) has dimension at most \(n-1\), so its proper image is a proper closed subset of \(W\).

Remove this image and the positive-dimensional-fiber locus of \(p\). On the remaining open the map is finite. Remove its non-étale locus as well; characteristic zero makes this another proper closed subset. Enlarge the union of the removed sets to a divisor \(E\). Then \(p^{-1}(W\setminus E)\) lies in \(V\) and is finite étale of positive degree \(m\) over \(W\setminus E\). The pullback of each global \(\alpha \in H^{n}(W)\) vanishes on \(V\), hence on this smaller open. Finite étale trace gives \(m\alpha |_{W\setminus E}=0\). Notice that no vanishing of all \(H^{n}(p^{-1}(W\setminus E))\) is asserted or needed. ∎

### Fano varieties

A smooth Fano variety is covered by rational curves. The same holds for a normal projective variety with ample \(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier anticanonical divisor; the covering curves may pass through its singular locus. These are consequences of the bend-and-break theorems in [Debarre, Theorems 7.5 and 7.7, Proposition 9.12 and Corollary 9.13](https://perso.imj-prg.fr/wp-content/uploads/debarre-pub/M22.pdf).

For Kawamata log terminal (klt) singularities, [Zhang, Proposition 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0408301) gives a stronger sufficient condition: if \(-K_W\) is nef and big, every smooth projective model of \(W\) is uniruled. Apply the proposition to the rational inverse of a resolution. This covers the quotient singularities of the weighted Fano varieties used below.

Here is how to apply the support theorem to a smooth projective model \(\widetilde W\) of such a variety. Choose an irreducible family of parametrized rational curves with dominant evaluation. A general curve has a unique rational lift to \(\widetilde W\), and properness extends that lift over all of \(\mathbb P^1\). Spread it over a smaller parameter open. A general slice of the parameter space gives a smooth affine \((n-1)\)-fold \(S\) and a dominant generically finite morphism \(\mathbb P^1\times S\to\widetilde W\). If the family was initially unparametrized, a finite base change splits its generic conic. The preceding proof and finite trace then give

\[
H^n(\widetilde W,\mathbb Q)=N^1H^n(\widetilde W,\mathbb Q).
\]

More generally, the same argument applies to every uniruled smooth projective \(n\)-fold. It is the existence of the covering family, rather than a particular rational curve or its equation, that supplies the cohomological conclusion.

### Degree-four Hodge classes

**Corollary.** If a smooth projective variety \(W\) satisfies \(H^4(W)=N^1H^4(W)\), every rational Hodge class in \(H^4(W)\) is algebraic. In particular this holds for a smooth Fano fourfold.

Indeed, the Gysin description in §3.1 gives a surjection of rational Hodge structures

\[
\bigoplus_i H^2(\widetilde D_i,\mathbb Q)(-1)\longrightarrow H^4(W,\mathbb Q)
\]

from resolutions of finitely many supporting divisors. Polarizable rational Hodge structures are semisimple: the polarization-orthogonal complement of the kernel gives a rational Hodge splitting. A rational \((2,2)\) class therefore lifts to rational \((1,1)\) classes on the \(\widetilde D_i\). Lefschetz's \((1,1)\) theorem makes these divisor classes; their Gysin images are algebraic codimension-two classes on \(W\). The Fano case follows from covering rational curves above. This also recovers the degree-four statement of the Conte–Murre theorem for uniruled fourfolds, recalled in [Murre, §§2.3–2.5](https://seminariomatematico.polito.it/rendiconti/71-34/473.pdf).

### Surface fibers with algebraic second cohomology

**Surface-fibration theorem.** Let \(W\) be a smooth projective fourfold admitting a dominant rational map to a surface whose geometric generic fiber has a smooth projective model \(T\) with \(p_g(T)=q(T)=0\). Assume the generic fiber is geometrically connected. Then
\[
H^4(W,\mathbb Q)=N^1H^4(W,\mathbb Q).
\]
The fiber need not be rational or uniruled.

**Proof.** Resolve the rational map and shrink its base to a smooth affine surface \(B\). Generic smoothness gives a smooth projective morphism \(f:V\to B\); after further shrinking its fibers have \(p_g=q=0\). Birational modifications and the omitted boundary change the support problem only by divisor-supported classes, as in §3.1.

The fibers have \(H^1=H^3=0\), and all of their rational \(H^2\) has type (1,1). Lefschetz's (1,1) theorem therefore makes it algebraic. Fix a relative ample class. Monodromy preserves this class and the integral intersection lattice; the Hodge index theorem makes its orthogonal complement negative definite. The integral isometry group of that complement is finite, so the local system \(R^2f_*\mathbb Q\) becomes constant after a finite étale base change.

Choose a basis of its divisor classes. After a further finite extension of the generic base field these classes are represented by line bundles: the relative Picard scheme has zero-dimensional identity component since \(q=0\), and the obstruction to realizing a Picard class by a line bundle is a Brauer class, split by a finite field extension. Spread finitely many such representatives and remove the branch and indeterminacy loci. We have a finite étale cover of a smaller affine \(B\), with global divisor classes \(d_1,\ldots,d_b\) on \(V\) restricting to a basis on every fiber. A square \(e\) of the relative ample class restricts nontrivially to fiber \(H^4\).

These global cycle classes give a Leray–Hirsch isomorphism
\[
Rf_*\mathbb Q\simeq
\mathbb Q\oplus\mathbb Q(-1)[-2]^b\oplus\mathbb Q(-2)[-4].
\]
For precision, map each shifted constant sheaf by the corresponding global cohomology class. On every stalk the maps give the basis in degrees zero, two and four, and the odd cohomology vanishes; their direct sum is therefore a quasi-isomorphism. In degree four this gives
\[
H^4(V)=H^4(B)\oplus\sum_i d_i\cup f^*H^2(B)
       \oplus e\,H^0(B).
\]
The first term is zero: algebraic de Rham cohomology of a smooth affine surface is computed by its complex of global differential forms, which ends in degree two. Every other term vanishes on the complement of the supports of the chosen divisors, including a divisor representing the ample class. Taking closures gives divisor support in a projective model. Finite étale trace sends this support to the original base; the deleted loci and the boundaries can also be included in a divisor. Pullback and pushforward through the birational modifications finish the proof. ∎

This uses the classical algebraicity of (1,1) classes on surfaces. It does not assume Bloch's conjecture for their zero-cycles, or an algebraic decomposition of their full Chow motives. After finite base change, the degree-four classes are supplied by the second cohomology of the base with a Tate twist and by algebraic fiber classes. The proof establishes existence of divisor support; explicit equations for those divisor families are additional data needed for a computed certificate.

## 3.3 Reflection quotients

**Reflection theorem.** Let \(X=\{F=0\}\) be a smooth sextic fourfold, with \(F\) even in a coordinate \(z\). For the reflection \(\sigma:z\mapsto-z\),
\[
H^4(X,\mathbb Q)^\sigma\subseteq N^1H^4(X,\mathbb Q).
\]
In particular, every residue with numerator odd in \(z\) is divisor-supported.

**Proof.** Write \(F(z,x)=H(z^{2},x_{1},\ldots ,x_{5})\). The quotient by \(\sigma\) is

\[
\begin{gathered}
W=\{H(u,x)=0\} \subset  \mathbb P(2,1,1,1,1,1).
\end{gathered}
\]

The coefficient of \(z^{6}\) cannot vanish: otherwise the \(z\)-axis point lies on \(X\) and all derivatives vanish there, because evenness forbids the only potentially relevant monomials \(z^{5}\cdot x_i\). Thus \(W\) misses the sole singular point of its weighted ambient space. On an ordinary chart \(x_i\ne 0\), if \(H\) and all its partials vanished, lifting \(u\) to \(z^{2}\) would make \(F\) and all its partials vanish. Hence \(W\) is smooth. Weighted adjunction gives \(-K_W=\mathcal O_W(1)\), an ample line bundle because \(W\) avoids the weighted singular point. Equivalently, Hurwitz gives \(\pi^{*}(-K_W)=\mathcal O_X(1)\), since \(K_X=0\) and the reflection branch divisor has class \(\mathcal O_X(1)\).

The Fano support theorem and quotient transfer give \(H^4(X)^\sigma\subseteq N^1H^4(X)\). The residue volume changes sign under \(\sigma\), so an odd numerator gives an invariant residue. ∎

**Three-reflection corollary.** If \(F\) is separately even in the three coordinates of either block, all of \(H^4(X)^\tau\) is divisor-supported. This is the diagonal-net case of [Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets); the two block-sign involutions agree projectively. It also follows from the finite-group argument below. Section 3.5 converts the support into certificate existence for every allowed numerator at every positive pole order.

### Finite groups generated by reflections

Let a finite linear \(G\) preserving \(F\) be generated by order-two hyperplane reflections, and assume \(\tau \in G\) or \(-\tau \in G\). The projector criterion of §3.1 has an elementary form here. Put \(U=\sum_s H^4(X)^s\), summing over the reflections. It is supported and \(G\)-stable. In \(H^4(X)/U\), every reflection acts by \(-1\), since \(v+s^*v\in H^4(X)^s\); hence \(G\) acts through its determinant character. Both \(\tau\) and \(-\tau\) have determinant \(-1\) in six variables and induce the same projective involution. Their invariant classes therefore lie in \(U\), proving all-target support. Mere normalization of \(G\) by \(\tau\) does not determine this last character and is insufficient. No commutativity assumption is needed.

The global involution has two fixed plane sextic curves, of codimension three in \(X\). Its transverse quotient singularities are \(\frac12(1,1,1)\). It supplies no branch divisor or Fano quotient of the kind used above; the nonuniruledness of this quotient and the resulting obstruction for its natural cubic cover are proved in §4.6.

### Finite quotients beyond reflections

Let \(g\) be a finite-order automorphism of a smooth projective Calabi–Yau variety. At a fixed point, write the tangent eigenvalues as \(\exp(2\pi i a_j)\), with \(0\le a_j<1\). Their sum is the *age* of the action at that point. If one fixed point has \(0<\sum a_j<1\), [Kollár–Larsen, Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701466) shows that the quotient by \(g\) is uniruled. A smooth projective resolution is therefore covered by rational curves. Slicing a dominating curve family gives the generically finite family required in §3.2; finite-quotient transfer then supports the \(g\)-invariant middle cohomology on a divisor.

For a smooth sextic fourfold, adjunction gives trivial canonical bundle, and Lefschetz gives simple connectivity and \(b_2=1\). The latter excludes a product of positive-dimensional projective varieties. Under these additional hypotheses [Kollár–Larsen, Corollary 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701466) strengthens the conclusion to rational connectedness. The support argument only needs uniruledness.

If a diagonal action fixes \(F\) exactly and has weights \(w_j\) modulo \(n\), a monomial numerator \(Z^e\) has residue character

\[
\sum_j(e_j+1)w_j\pmod n.
\]

The added ones record the volume determinant. Thus invariance of the polynomial numerator alone is not the relevant test. The averaging ideal of §3.1 combines the supported residue spaces and their group translates. The cover construction in §2.7 can reach further characters because its useful reflection acts on an auxiliary variety rather than on the original fourfold.

## 3.4 Nonlinear polynomial Piola maps are finite Fano maps

**Theorem.** Let \(\Phi =(\Phi _{1},\ldots ,\Phi _{6})\) be homogeneous polynomials with degrees \(m_{i}\), put \(M=\sum m_{i}\) and \(\delta =\operatorname{det}(d\Phi )\), and suppose

\[
\begin{gathered}
1\le m_{i}\le 5,       7\le M\le 12,       F=G(\Phi ),       \operatorname{wt}(G)=6,\\
X=\{F=0\} \;\text{smooth}\;.
\end{gathered}
\]

Then \(\Phi \) is finite and \(W=\{G=0\}\subset \mathbb P(m_{1},\ldots ,m_{6})\) is a normal Fano fourfold with quotient singularities. For every \(q\ge 1\) and weighted polynomial \(b\) of weight \(6(q+1)-M\), the residue target \(A=\delta b(\Phi )\) is divisor-supported and has a certificate. In the involution problem retain the required odd target parity. No spectral derivation or eigencondition on \(b\) is assumed.

### Finiteness and quasismoothness

No variable has weight six, so \(G\) has no constant or ordinary linear term. A nonzero common zero \(z\) of the \(\Phi _{i}\) would satisfy \(F(z)=0\) and \(\nabla F(z)=d\Phi (z)^{T}\nabla G(0)=0\). Thus the \(\Phi _{i}\) have only the origin as common affine zero. They form a homogeneous system of parameters: choose homogeneous representatives of a basis of the finite-dimensional quotient \(k[Z]/(\Phi _{1},\ldots ,\Phi _{6})\), and induct on degree to see that these representatives generate \(k[Z]\) over \(k[\Phi ]\). Consequently the affine map \(\Phi \) is finite and surjective, the six \(\Phi _{i}\) are algebraically independent, and \(\delta \ne 0\) in characteristic zero. The induced projective map \(\pi :X\to W\) is finite and surjective.

If \(y\ne 0\) were a critical zero of \(G\), finite surjectivity would supply \(z\ne 0\) with \(\Phi (z)=y\), and the chain rule would make \(z\) a singular point of \(F\). Hence the cone of \(G\) is smooth away from its vertex: \(W\) is quasismooth.

### The coarse canonical class

For well-formed weights, a quasismooth weighted complete intersection of dimension at least three is well formed unless an equation degree equals an ambient weight. This is the well-formedness theorem recalled in [Sano–Tasin, §1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.15209). Here degree six exceeds every weight. Weighted adjunction therefore gives \(-K_W=\mathcal O_W(M-6)\), ample and \(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier. Quasismoothness gives quotient singularities. The weighted adjunction and residue facts used here are classical; see [Dolgachev, §§3.3 and 4.2–4.3](https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/idolga/wp-content/uploads/sites/1334/2024/08/weighted82.pdf).

There are two exceptional ambient profiles: (1,2,2,2,2,2) and (2,2,2,2,2,2). Indeed, a non-well-formed six-tuple has some five weights divisible by an integer \(a\ge 2\). Their sum is at least \(5\cdot a\), so \(M\le 12\) forces \(a=2\); with weights at most five, those five must all equal two. The sixth can only be one or two. In the first profile, every monomial of \(G\) is even in the weight-one variable \(t\). Set \(u=t^{2}\); the second Veronese identifies \(W\) with an ordinary cubic \(R(u,t_{1},\ldots ,t_{5})=0\) in \(\mathbb P^{5}\). A nonzero critical zero of \(R\) lifts to one of \(G\), so this cubic is smooth. Regrading the all-two profile gives the same conclusion. In both cases the coarse anticanonical class is six times the old rational hyperplane class, at least \(M-6\). This explicit check avoids confusing the weighted-stack canonical class with the coarse one along a divisorial stabilizer.

### The target is a global residue pullback

Let \(\Omega _z\) be contraction of the six-variable volume form with the ordinary Euler field, and \(\Omega _m\) contraction with \(\sum m_{i}t_{i}\partial _{t_{i}}\). Homogeneity gives \(d\Phi (\epsilon _z)=\epsilon _m\circ \Phi \). Contracting \(\Phi^*(\mathrm dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathrm dt_6)=\delta\,\mathrm dz_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathrm dz_6\) therefore gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
\Phi^{*}(\Omega _m)=\delta \Omega _z,\\
\Phi^{*}(b\Omega _m/G^{q+1})=\delta b(\Phi )\Omega _z/F^{q+1}.
\end{gathered}
\]

The weight condition makes the downstairs form homogeneous of weight zero and horizontal for the weighted Euler field. It is a global closed form on the complement of \(G=0\) in the smooth weighted projective stack. Residue gives a global \(H^{4}\) class on its smooth hypersurface stack. This may also be constructed on finite quotient charts: ordinary residues commute with the chart group and glue. Rational cohomology of a finite stabilizer vanishes in positive degrees, so the cohomology of the stack equals that of its coarse space. Thus there is a global \(\beta \in H^{4}(W)\) with \(\alpha _A=\pi^{*}\beta \). We have not assumed that an arbitrary class on \(W_{\mathrm{reg}}\) extends across its singularities.

Pull \(\beta \) to a projective resolution \(\widetilde{W}\). The Fano support theorem gives divisor support for all \(H^{4}(\widetilde{W})\). Remove from \(W\) the images of that support and the exceptional locus; on the remainder the resolution is an isomorphism and \(\beta \) vanishes. Their inverse images under \(\pi \) are proper closed subsets of \(X\) and can be enlarged to a divisor. This proves the target assertion, including its global extension and boundary terms. ∎

### Why every primitive nonlinear polynomial atom is included

For a \(q=1\) polynomial Piola target \(A=b(\Phi )\delta \) of degree six, homogeneity gives \(\operatorname{wt}(b)=12-M\), so \(6\le M\le 12\). A nonlinear \(\Phi \) has \(M>6\). A weight at least seven forces the profile (7,1,1,1,1,1); then \(G\) ignores that coordinate and \(F\) depends on only five linear forms, contradicting smoothness.

If a weight is six, write \(G=c\cdot t_j+H\), with \(c\) constant. If \(c=0\), the other five positive-degree forms have a common nonzero zero, while their weights are at most two. Since \(H\) has no ordinary linear term, that zero is singular for \(F\). Thus \(c\ne 0\). The polynomial field

\[
\begin{gathered}
B=b(\Phi ) \operatorname{adj}(d\Phi )\cdot e_j/c
\end{gathered}
\]

has degree one and satisfies \(B(F)=A\). Consequently \(A\) lies in the degree-six Jacobian ideal. In the invariant \(q=1\) problem, parity averaging makes \(\operatorname{div}B\) a \(Y\)-odd constant, hence zero. This case is already polynomial and has zero primitive target. Every nonzero primitive nonlinear polynomial atom must therefore satisfy the theorem's degree hypotheses. Linear maps and arbitrary rational adapted maps are not covered by this argument.

Six arbitrary globally \(Y\)-even quadrics composed with any cubic \(G\) illustrate the theorem: \(\delta \) is an odd sextic, and its class pulls back from a smooth cubic fourfold. This is distinct from the cubic-surface construction over passive ratios. More generally, all determinant densities on the same finite map are supported even when a chosen spectral-field constructor serves only a smaller sector. For the special map \((X,Y)\mapsto(X,Q_0(Y),Q_1(Y),Q_2(Y))\), [Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets) proves support for the entire \(\tau\)-invariant fourth cohomology.

## 3.5 From divisor support to every pole order

For \(1\le q\le4\), the support-to-certificate theorem of [Chapter 1](#technical-information/certificates) converts divisor support of the residue class into a legal rational primitive. A supporting divisor can be enlarged to the zero set of a homogeneous polynomial \(D\) with \(F\nmid D\). Coefficient descent and averaging give the ground-field and involution conditions when required. The same support suffices for all larger pole orders by the following algebraic reduction.

For \(q\ge 5\), the regular sequence of six quintic partials has Jacobian-ring socle degree 24. Hence \(A=\sum B_{i}F_{i}\) for homogeneous \(B_{i}\) of degree \(6\cdot q-5\). Average \(B\) to impose parity and put \(c=\operatorname{div} B\). If \(w\) serves \((q-1,c)\), direct differentiation gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=(B+F\cdot w)/q,\\
K_q(A;v)=(F/q)K_{q-1}(c;w).
\end{gathered}
\]

This inducts to \(q\le4\) without enlarging the supporting divisor. Thus an all-class geometric support theorem yields certificate existence at every positive pole order.

## 3.6 Supported projectors in families

The curve and surface arguments above construct support on a total space. A third input is a fiberwise algebraic projector with a representative supported on the square of a divisor. Two lemmas explain how such representatives specialize and spread. Fiberwise coniveau alone does not provide these conclusions: the projector and its support must be parametrized together, and the relative argument below uses concentration in one cohomological degree.

### Specialization

**Supported-projector specialization.** Let \(p:\mathcal X\to B\) be a smooth projective family of \(n\)-folds over a smooth connected complex algebraic base. Let \(P\) be a relative rational algebraic correspondence of codimension \(n\), whose restrictions are projectors. Suppose that, at a very general \(b\), its cohomology class has a representative \(Z_b\) supported on \(D_b\times D_b\), for a divisor \(D_b\subset X_b\). Then such a representative exists at every \(b\in B\).

**Proof.** Write a positive integral multiple of \(Z_b\) as a difference of effective cycles. Parametrize the divisor and these cycles by relative flag Hilbert schemes, imposing the closed incidence conditions that the cycles lie in the divisor's square. There are countably many choices of Hilbert polynomials and integral multiplicities. Each resulting parameter space is proper over \(B\). On each connected component, the equality of the cycle class with the same multiple of \([P_b]\) is locally constant: universal flat cycles give flat sections of the pulled-back cohomology local system of the smooth ambient family.

The component through a representative at a very general point cannot have image contained in a proper closed subset of \(B\). Its image is closed by properness, so it is all of \(B\). The same cohomological identity holds at every point of this component. The fixed Hilbert polynomial of the divisor keeps its support of dimension \(n-1\) after specialization; the flag condition keeps the cycle on its square. Dividing by the chosen integral multiple gives the required rational cycle on every fiber. ∎

The hypothesis asks for equality of cohomology classes, not rational equivalence of projectors. No decomposition of the Chow motive is asserted. Chapter 3B obtains this hypothesis from a curve correspondence and a polynomial inverse on its Hodge-theoretic image.

### Relative support over a curve

**Relative support lemma.** Let \(p:\mathcal T\to U\) be a smooth projective family of threefolds over a smooth complex curve, with a fiberwise algebraic involution \(\sigma\). Suppose

\[
(R^jp_*\mathbb Q)^-=0\quad(j\ne3),
\]

and the anti-projector \(P^-_u=(\Delta_{T_u}-\Gamma_{\sigma_u})/2\) has a cycle representative supported on \(D_u\times D_u\) at every fiber. After removing finitely many points of \(U\), one divisor in \(\mathcal T\) supports \(H^4(\mathcal T,\mathbb Q)^-\). Its closure together with the omitted fibers supports any global class on a smooth projective model whose restriction is anti-invariant.

**Proof.** The flag parameter spaces from the preceding lemma have countably many proper images covering \(U\). One component dominates \(U\). A multisection and normalization give a finite extension of its function field; after shrinking, this is a finite étale cover \(U'\to U\). On the pulled-back family there are a relative divisor \(D'\) and a relative cycle \(Z'\), supported on \(D'\times_{U'}D'\), whose fiber classes equal the anti-projector. Push \(Z'\) along the finite map of relative products and divide by the cover degree. This gives a rational relative cycle \(Z\) over \(U\) with the same fiber classes, supported on \(D\times_U D\), where \(D\) is the finite image of \(D'\). Enlarge \(D\) by its involution image.

Apply \((1-\sigma)/2\) on both factors to \(Z\). This preserves its support and fiber classes and makes its global class anti-invariant in both factors. Let

\[
r:\mathcal T\times_U\mathcal T\longrightarrow U,
\qquad V=(R^3p_*\mathbb Q)^-.
\]

Relative Künneth and the concentration assumption give

\[
(R^kr_*\mathbb Q)^{--}=0\ (k\ne6),\qquad
(R^6r_*\mathbb Q)^{--}=V\otimes V.
\]

The Leray spectral sequence therefore identifies

\[
H^6(\mathcal T\times_U\mathcal T,\mathbb Q)^{--}
\simeq H^0(U,V\otimes V).
\]

In particular, a class in this double-anti-invariant part is determined by its restrictions to the fibers. Both \([Z]\) and the class of the relative anti-projector lie in that part, so their fiberwise equality gives \([Z]=[P^-]\) globally. Their correspondence actions on \(H^4(\mathcal T)\) agree. The action of \(P^-\) is the identity on

\[
H^4(\mathcal T)^-\simeq H^1(U,V),
\]

whereas the action of \(Z\) vanishes after restriction to \(\mathcal T\setminus D\), because its target support is in \(D\). This proves support on the open family. Taking closures and adjoining the boundary divisors proves the last assertion; proper birational pushforward transfers it to another smooth projective model, as in §3.1. ∎

The three fibration inputs now have distinct roles. Rational curves kill cohomology on an affine open. Surface fibers with \(p_g=q=0\) supply global divisor classes and a Leray–Hirsch decomposition after finite base change. The relative support lemma uses a supported projector and a single nonzero anti-invariant cohomology degree. They share the same transfer and boundary arguments, but their hypotheses are not interchangeable.

# 3. Geometric support, finite groups and surface fibrations

[Previous: binary sextics and torsion contacts](#technical-information/binary-blocks) · [Contents](#technical-information/introduction) · [Next: split sextics and K3 correspondences](#technical-information/split-and-k3)

A certificate constructs a primitive on the complement of a divisor. Geometry establishes the same vanishing through Gysin maps and correspondences. This chapter develops the shared tools: finite quotients, correspondences over a common base, two-forms on curve families, covering rational curves, surface fibrations with \(p_g=q=0\), and supported projectors in families. The reflection and relative-projector results supply the two parts of [Chapter 3B](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds). Fano support and correspondence transfer also underlie the quadratic-net theorem of [Chapter 3C](#technical-information/quadratic-nets). Work in characteristic zero; cohomology is rational, or algebraic de Rham after scalar extension.

## 3.1 Divisor support and its source

For a smooth projective variety \(X\), a class is divisor-supported if it vanishes on \(X\setminus Z\) for some divisor \(Z\). The resulting subspace is \(N^{1}H^{k}(X)\). Here is the Gysin description of that space. Take an embedded resolution \(r:\widetilde{X}\to X\) whose reduced inverse image \(E=\bigcup E_i\) is a simple normal-crossing divisor. Localization places \(r^{*}\alpha \) in the image of \(H^{k}_E(\widetilde{X})\to H^{k}(\widetilde{X})\). The Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence for supports and purity give, for an intersection of \(c\) components, the terms \(H^{k-c-1}(E_{i_{1}}\cap \cdots \cap E_{i_c})(-c)\) contributing to degree \(k\). Their weights are \(k+c-1\). The \(c=1\) terms have weight \(k\), while all deeper intersections have larger weight. Strictness of mixed-Hodge morphisms therefore makes the image in the pure \(H^{k}(\widetilde{X})\) equal to the image of \(\sum _i H^{k-2}(E_i)(-1)\). Push forward and use \(r_*r^{*}=\operatorname{id}\). This proves that \(N^{1}H^{k}(X)\) is generated by the resulting proper Gysin images from smooth divisors. The localization, purity and strictness inputs are stated in [Chapter 1](#technical-information/certificates).

On a fourfold the (3,1) part must consequently come from \(H^{2,0}(E_i)\). Components contracted into codimension at least two have zero (3,1) image: degree-four classes supported in codimension two come from degree-zero classes of surfaces with twist \((-2)\), and hence have type (2,2). Thus resolutions of the actual divisor components supply the relevant holomorphic two-forms. A count of singularities or contact multiplicities does not determine their Gysin map.

On a smooth sextic fourfold this forces singularities on any divisor supporting a nonzero (3,1) class. Lefschetz gives \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=\mathbb Z[\mathcal O_X(1)]\), so every nonzero effective divisor \(D\) is ample. The sequence \(0\to\mathcal O_X(-D)\to\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_D\to0\), the vanishing \(H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0\), and Kodaira vanishing with Serre duality give \(H^2(D,\mathcal O_D)=0\). If \(D\) is normal with rational singularities, a resolution \(\widetilde D\to D\) has the same coherent cohomology, hence \(H^{2,0}(\widetilde D)=0\). Such a component has zero (3,1) Gysin image. Therefore a support for a nonzero (3,1) class must contain a component which is nonnormal or has nonrational singularities. In particular, replacing a support by a smooth divisor need not preserve its cohomological role.

Support is stable under finite sums: take the union of the supports. For a dominant generically finite proper morphism between smooth varieties of the same dimension, pullback and pushforward preserve divisor support. Pullback uses the inverse image of a support; pushforward uses its proper image, which still has codimension at least one. The degree identity \(p_*p^{*}=\operatorname{deg}(p) \operatorname{id}\) follows from the projection formula.

If a finite group \(G\) acts on a variety \(M\), rational cohomology of the quotient is the invariant cohomology. One proof uses the finite quotient map \(\pi \): the invariant part of \(\pi _*\mathbb Q\) is the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q\), higher direct images vanish, and taking \(G\)-invariants is exact over \(\mathbb Q\). When \(M\) and the quotient are smooth, the corresponding identities are

\[
\begin{gathered}
\pi _*\pi^{*} = |G| \operatorname{id},             \pi^{*}\pi _* = \sum _{g\in G} g^{*}.
\end{gathered}
\]

They also hold for branched quotients: the top-dimensional cycle of \(M\times _{M/G}M\) is the sum of the graphs of the group elements. Their intersections over the branch locus do not add a top-dimensional component.

**Quotient-transfer lemma.** Let \(M\) be smooth projective with a faithful finite \(G\)-action, and let \(N\) be a smooth projective model of \(M/G\). Then \(H^{k}(N)\) is divisor-supported if and only if \(H^{k}(M)^G\) is divisor-supported.

**Proof.** Resolve the quotient rational map equivariantly as \(r:R\to M\) and \(p:R\to N\). Here \(r\) is a sequence of blowups with smooth centers and \(p\) is generically finite of degree \(|G|\). The blowup decomposition

\[
\begin{gathered}
H^{k}(\operatorname{Bl}_C M) = H^{k}(M) \oplus  \bigoplus _{j=1}^{\operatorname{codim} C-1} H^{k-2\cdot j}(C)(-j)
\end{gathered}
\]

shows that \(\operatorname{ker} r_*\) is supported on the exceptional divisors. For this formula, write the exceptional divisor as \(E=\mathbb P(N_{C/M})\) and \(\xi =c_{1}(\mathcal O_E(1))\). The added summands map by \(\gamma \mapsto i_*(\xi ^{j-1}\pi^{*}\gamma )\). The projective-bundle decomposition of \(H^{*}(E)\), together with the localization comparison across \(\operatorname{Bl}_C M\setminus E\cong M\setminus C\), gives the displayed decomposition; \(r_*r^{*}=\operatorname{id}\) splits off \(H^{k}(M)\). If \(H^{k}(M)^G\) is supported, then \(r_*p^{*}\beta \) is supported for every \(\beta \in H^{k}(N)\). Hence \(r^{*}r_*p^{*}\beta \) is supported, and \(p^{*}\beta \) differs from it by an exceptional class. Push forward and divide by \(|G|\) to support \(\beta \).

Conversely, take \(\alpha \in H^{k}(M)^G\) and assume \(H^{k}(N)\) is supported. The class \(p^{*}p_*r^{*}\alpha \) is supported. Over the dense open where \(p\) is the finite group quotient, transfer identifies it with \(\sum _g g^{*}r^{*}\alpha =|G|r^{*}\alpha \). Their difference is supported on the omitted boundary, which can be included in a divisor. Push forward by \(r\) and divide by \(|G|\). This proves the lemma and explains why the boundary cannot be dropped. The same proof shows invariance of the all-supported assertion under smooth projective birational modification. ∎

These constructions use algebraic graphs, blowups and traces. An abstract Hodge isomorphism alone would not transport a supporting equation.

### Correspondences over a common base

Let \(M,N\) be smooth projective varieties of the same dimension \(d\). A \(d\)-cycle \(C\subset M\times N\) whose components dominate both factors preserves divisor support:
\[
C_*\bigl(N^1H^k(M)\bigr)\subseteq N^1H^k(N).
\]
Resolve each component of \(C\). Both projections are proper and generically finite. The inverse image of a supporting divisor has dimension at most \(d-1\), and its proper image has dimension at most \(d-1\) as well. Pullback and pushforward through this resolution give the asserted correspondence action. The same argument applies componentwise when \(N\) is disconnected.

**Common-base boundary lemma.** Suppose smooth projective \(d\)-folds \(M_i\) have dominant morphisms to one projective variety \(B\), and all correspondences under consideration lie in the relative products \(M_i\times_B M_j\). Let \(B^\circ\subset B\) be dense open and \(M_i^\circ=M_i\times_B B^\circ\). An identity between the restricted correspondences, or their composites, gives the same identity on global cohomology modulo classes supported on the complement of the output open.

Indeed, if the output point lies over \(B^\circ\), the relative-product condition forces every intermediate point and the input point to lie over \(B^\circ\). Restriction therefore commutes with each proper correspondence action and with its composites. The error operator has image in
\[
\ker\bigl(H^k(M_j)\longrightarrow H^k(M_j^\circ)\bigr).
\]
The complement is a proper closed subset and can be included in a divisor. This proves the claim. The common base is essential to this argument: equality on an arbitrary product open alone does not control contributions from the omitted source.

### Averaging projectors and the part served by a quotient

Let a finite group \(G\) act on a smooth projective variety \(M\), and write
\[
e_K=\frac1{|K|}\sum_{k\in K}k\in\mathbb Q[G]
\]
for a subgroup \(K\). Use \(g\mapsto(g^{-1})^*\) for the left action on cohomology; averaging has the same image under either pullback convention. Suppose smooth projective models of \(M/K_1,\ldots,M/K_s\) have divisor-supported \(H^m\). Form the two-sided ideal
\[
I=\sum_j\mathbb Q[G]e_{K_j}\mathbb Q[G].
\]
Then
\[
I H^m(M)\subseteq N^1H^m(M).
\]
Indeed, quotient transfer supports \(e_{K_j}H^m(M)=H^m(M)^{K_j}\), and \(N^1\) is stable under every group element and under finite sums. This proves the assertion for each product \(a e_{K_j}b\) and hence for \(I\).

Maschke's theorem makes the scope exact at the representation-theoretic level. A simple rational representation \(\rho\) occurs in the ideal \(I\) precisely when \(\rho^{K_j}\ne0\) for at least one \(j\): in its simple algebra factor, \(e_{K_j}\) is nonzero exactly under that condition, and any nonzero element generates the factor as a two-sided ideal. Thus the supported invariant spaces, together with their \(G\)-translates, serve the entire isotypic component of every such \(\rho\). Any projector lying in \(I\) has supported image. This is a criterion for these quotients, not an assertion that the remaining representations lack support from other correspondences.

The same argument applies on a finite auxiliary cover. Resolve a projective model equivariantly, compute the ideal there, and use the proper generically finite map to the original variety. A physical class is served when its pullback lies in the supported image; normalized pushforward then descends the support. Reflections, deck traces and exchanges are instances of this one procedure. Finding more curves on a fixed quotient improves its construction, but cannot add a representation absent from its averaging projector.

### Descent through a deck action and an exchange

Quotients of an auxiliary cover can support complementary parts of the original variety's cohomology. The following criterion isolates the relations needed for their combined descent.

**Proposition.** Let \(p:Z\to X\) be a proper dominant generically finite morphism of smooth complex projective varieties. Let \(d,g\) be finite-order automorphisms of \(Z,X\), respectively; let \(r,\sigma\) be commuting involutions of \(Z\), and \(\tau\) an involution of \(X\). Put \(e=\sigma d\sigma\), and suppose
\[
pd=p,\qquad pe=gp,\qquad pr=\tau p.
\]
If smooth projective models of \(Z/\langle r,\sigma\rangle\) and \(X/\langle g\rangle\) have divisor-supported \(H^k\), then
\[
H^k(X,\mathbb Q)^\tau\subseteq N^1H^k(X,\mathbb Q).
\]

**Proof.** Quotient transfer in §3.1 supports the corresponding invariant spaces. Take \(\xi\in H^k(X)^\tau\), and write \(a=p^*\xi\) in
\[
V=H^k(Z)/N^1H^k(Z).
\]
Then \(d^*a=r^*a=a\). Since \(r,\sigma\) commute, \(p^*\xi+\sigma^*p^*\xi\) is invariant under both; its image \(a+\sigma^*a\) is therefore zero in \(V\). Thus \(\sigma^*a=-a\), which gives
\[
e^*a=\sigma^*d^*\sigma^*a=a.
\]
Let \(\operatorname{Av}_h\) denote averaging over a finite cyclic action. The relation \(pe=gp\) and dominance of \(p\) imply that the order of \(g\) divides that of \(e\), so
\[
a=\operatorname{Av}_e a=p^*(\operatorname{Av}_g\xi)=0
\quad\text{in }V.
\]
The last equality follows from support of \(H^k(X)^{\langle g\rangle}\). Finally, proper pushforward preserves divisor support and \(p_*p^*\xi=\deg(p)\xi\). This proves the claim. ∎

For a rational presentation, apply the criterion after exhibiting a finite symmetry group and resolving its action together with the cover projection equivariantly. Finiteness is a hypothesis to check; individual birational symmetries do not by themselves supply the required models.

## 3.2 Curve correspondences and fibrations

Families of curves on a fourfold give divisor support through their cylinder correspondences. Their action on \(H^{3,1}\) can be tested by a normal-bundle pairing. A covering family of rational curves gives a different conclusion by vanishing on an affine open. Surface fibers with \(p_g=q=0\) give that vanishing after removing finitely many relative divisor classes. These constructions share the support and transfer arguments of §3.1.

### Two-forms on curve families

Let \(X\) be a smooth complex projective fourfold, and let \(\mathcal C\subset S\times X\) be a flat algebraic family whose fibers are smooth connected curves over a dense open of the smooth parameter variety \(S\). The universal cycle associates to \(\omega\in H^{3,1}(X)\) a closed two-form \(\beta_\omega\) on that open. On a smooth projective parameter space its class is the cylinder pullback \(p_*e^*\omega\in H^{2,0}(S)\), where \(p,e\) are the projections of the universal curve.

When \(K_X\simeq\mathcal O_X\), this form has a useful obstruction-theoretic expression. Fix a nonvanishing volume form \(\Omega_X\), embed \(X\) as a smooth divisor in a smooth fivefold \(P\), and let \(C\) be one of the curves. Put \(N=N_{C/X}\), and write

\[
0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow N_{C/P}
\longrightarrow N_{X/P}|_C\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
\delta_C:H^0(C,N_{X/P}|_C)\longrightarrow H^1(C,N).
\]

A section \(A\in H^0(X,N_{X/P})\) gives an embedded Kodaira–Spencer class \(\kappa_A\in H^1(X,T_X)\). Set \(\omega_A=\kappa_A\mathbin{\lrcorner}\Omega_X\). Adjunction identifies \(\det N\) with \(K_C\). For tangent vectors to \(S\) whose normal sections are \(s,t\in H^0(C,N)\),

\[
\boxed{\quad
\beta_{\omega_A}(s,t)
=\operatorname{Tr}_C\bigl(s\wedge t\wedge\delta_C(A|_C)\bigr).
\quad}
\]

The equality uses a fixed choice of signs and normalization of the cycle class. Its nonvanishing is independent of that choice. Equivalently, the right side pairs \(\delta_C(A|_C)\) with \(s\wedge t\in H^0(C,N^\vee\otimes K_C)\) by Serre duality.

**Proof of the formula.** The Hilbert-scheme formula of [Kuznetsov–Markushevich, Theorem 6.1 and formula (25)](https://homepage.mi-ras.ru/~akuznet/publications/SymplecticStructuresOnModuliSpacesOfSheavesViaTheAtyiahClass.pdf) pairs \(s,t,\omega_A|_C\) with the conormal inclusion \(N^\vee\to\Omega_X^1|_C\). For a curve in a fourfold there is one copy of that inclusion. Contracting \(\kappa_A|_C\) with \(\Omega_X\), then applying the conormal inclusion, gives the projection of \(\kappa_A|_C\) to \(H^1(C,N)\), with values in \(\det N\). Naturality of the tangent and normal exact sequences identifies this projection with \(\delta_C(A|_C)\). Wedge with \(s,t\), use \(\det N\simeq K_C\), and take the Serre trace. This is also the infinitesimal expression for the universal-cycle pullback, so it holds after pullback to any smooth algebraic family of curves. ∎

**Curve-family support criterion.** If \(\beta_\omega\) is nonzero on an actual algebraic family, there are a smooth projective surface \(T\) and a cycle \(\Gamma\in\operatorname{CH}^3(T\times X)_{\mathbb Q}\) such that \(\Gamma^*\omega\ne0\) in \(H^{2,0}(T)\). The image of

\[
\Gamma_*:H^2(T,\mathbb Q)(-1)\longrightarrow H^4(X,\mathbb Q)
\]

is divisor-supported and has nonzero \((3,1)\) part.

**Proof.** Close the image of \(S\) in the projective Hilbert scheme of \(X\), take a reduced irreducible component on which the form is nonzero, and resolve it to \(\widetilde M\). Pulling back the universal flat curve gives a cycle in \(\operatorname{CH}^3(\widetilde M\times X)\). Its action gives a global class in \(H^{2,0}(\widetilde M)\) restricting to the displayed two-form. Thus extension across the parameter boundary is supplied by the universal cycle. A general smooth complete-intersection surface \(T\subset\widetilde M\) retains the nonzero class, by weak Lefschetz. Restrict the universal cycle to obtain \(\Gamma\).

Every component of \(\Gamma\) has dimension three, so its proper image in \(X\) is contained in a divisor. Its action therefore vanishes on the complement of that divisor. If \(\eta=\Gamma^*\omega\ne0\), the nonzero pairing \(\int_T\eta\wedge\overline\eta\) equals \(\int_X\omega\wedge\Gamma_*\overline\eta\). Hence \(\Gamma_*\overline\eta\) is a nonzero \((1,3)\) class; conjugation gives the asserted \((3,1)\) image. ∎

This criterion detects a nonzero supported image; at a fixed fourfold it does not assert that the particular input \(\omega\) belongs to that image. For invariant \(\omega\), replace \(\Gamma\) by its average under the involution on \(X\). The pullback of \(\omega\) remains nonzero, and the new image is invariant. [Chapter 4, §4.4](#technical-information/known-locus) gives the further conclusion available when the curve construction dominates the even-sextic coefficient space.

### Vanishing tests for the normal pairing

The normal sections must come from actual motions in a family. A two-dimensional Zariski tangent space at an obstructed point alone does not supply them. On a curve of genus \(g\) in a fourfold with trivial canonical bundle, adjunction and Riemann–Roch give

\[
\chi(N)=1-g.
\]

Thus two independent sections require \(h^1(N)\ge g+1\). A nonzero obstruction space is compatible with a smooth parameter family; requiring \(H^1(N)=0\) would instead make every displayed pairing zero.

**Example: complete-intersection curves.** Suppose \(C=V_X(G_1,G_2,G_3)\) is a smooth complete intersection in a smooth sextic \(X\subset\mathbb P^5\), with \(G_i\) homogeneous of degrees \(d_i\). The regular sequence \((F,G_1,G_2,G_3)\) identifies

\[
N_{C/\mathbb P^5}
\simeq\mathcal O_C(6)\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^3\mathcal O_C(d_i),
\]

and the normal map to \(\mathcal O_C(6)\) is projection to the first summand. Its connecting map \(\delta_C\) is zero. Hence \(\beta_{\omega_A}\) vanishes on every pair of Hilbert tangent directions at \(C\), for every sextic numerator \(A\). This conclusion concerns the whole normal pairing, including motions outside the evident complete-intersection presentation.

**Ambient sections and residual curves.** Let \(T\) be smooth projective, let \(Z\in\operatorname{CH}^2(T\times X)_{\mathbb Q}\) be the class of a family of surfaces, and let \(h\) be a polarization on \(X\). A curve correspondence of the form

\[
\Gamma=(d\,\operatorname{pr}_X^*h+\operatorname{pr}_T^*\ell)\cdot Z,
\qquad \ell\in\operatorname{CH}^1(T),
\]

kills \(H^{3,1}(X)_{\mathrm{prim}}\). Indeed, the projection formula gives

\[
\Gamma^*\alpha=d\,Z^*(h\alpha)+\ell\cup Z^*\alpha=0:
\]
